people.biosketch: Prof. Attila Aszódi is the scientific coordinator of the Musculoskeletal University Center Munich (MUM) (MUM) and head of the "Cartilage Development, Diseases, and Regulation" group at LMU University Hospital in Munich. His research focuses on musculoskeletal tissues, particularly cartilage development, diseases, and regeneration. His main area of interest is identifying the effects of integrin-mediated cell-matrix interactions and Rho GTPase signaling cascades on cartilage physiology and pathophysiology. In addition, he investigates the role of extracellular matrix integrity in regulating the development, function, and regeneration of the skeletal system. His group's research explored the role of beta1 integrins and matrilin family of ECM proteins in joint development and cartilage homeostasis. His laboratory uses a multidisciplinary approach—combining mouse genetics, stem cell biology, and biomechanical studies—to study the processes of cartilage differentiation and repair, with a particular focus on diseases such as osteoarthritis.

institution: Laboratoire Interuniversitaire de Biologie de la Motricité

people.biosketch: Dr Charles-Étienne Benoit has been recruited since 2021 at the University Claude Bernard Lyon 1 as an associate-professor in the Inter-University Laboratory of Motricity Biology (LIBM). His research activities focus on the study of rhythm and music on the motor and cognitive abilities of healthy and pathological individuals. He is interested in motor learning, cognitive fatigue, sleep, the impact of breathing and endogenous rhythms on memory, the impact of technology on mental or physical health. All with a strong interest in cognitive behavioral sciences, neuroplasticity, pharmacology and applied neuroscience.

Christophe Hautier is an exercise physiology and biomechanics researcher, lecturer at the University Claude Bernard Lyon 1. He is currently head of the Laboratoire Interuniversitaire de Biologie de la Motricité of Lyon. Christophe Hautier's research activity focuses on the neuromuscular determinants of motor performance and injury risk from patients to high-level athletes. Christophe Hautier has published 65 articles (citations > 3000, H index 30). Christophe Hautier manages a FUI project financed by European FEDER funds about the influence of soft tissues vibrations generated by sports practice on fatigue and muscle damage with a view to developing innovative solutions for damping vibrations.

Pr Vincent Pialoux is an exercise physiologist, Professor at University Claude Bernard Lyon 1. He is leader of the Team Atherosclerosis, Thrombosis and Physical Activity (ATPA) of the inter-university Laboratory of Human Movement Biology. His general research area investigates the biological mechanisms of physical activity in the context of vascular diseases and Cancer. He is founded by the Institut Universitaire de France, the France-Canada Research Fund, the Federation Française de Cardiologie, the Société Française d'Athérosclérose, the Ligue contre le Cancer and the Fondation ARC pour la Recherche sur le Cancer. He has published 141 articles (cited > 4400 times and H index 37).

Bert Blaauw is professor in physiology at the University of Padova and a principal investigator at the Venetian Institute of Molecular Medicine in Padova. His main research interests are on the signaling pathways regulating adult skeletal muscle mass and function, and how these pathways are affected by exercise. His group has published multiple papers expanding the knowledge on the intracellular pathways regulating skeletal muscle mass and force. The major focus in his work has been on the Akt-mTORC1 pathway and he has contributed to better understanding its role as one of the major pathways regulating adult skeletal muscle size and function. Importantly, he showed that muscle mTOR signaling is critical in maintaining a proper nerve-muscle interaction. During the last years he focused his attention on how this pathway is altered in cancer cachexia, and more importantly how reactivation of this signaling pathway can completely revert the muscle wasting observed in cancer cachexia

Dr. Leonardo Nogara is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Biomedical Sciences at the University of Padua (Italy), working in the Muscle Contractility and Neuromuscular Plasticity unit. He has experience measuring muscle contractility at different scales, from in vivo murine models to ex vivo isolated muscle preparations, down to single muscle fibers mechanically isolated. His work centers on the Super Relaxed State (SRX) of myosin, the main skeletal muscle motor protein. Muscle tissue experiences about a 100-fold increase in metabolic load ranging from rest to active exercise; in this context, the SRX is a biochemical state evolved as an energy-saving mechanism. To explore the physiological and pathological effects of SRX modulation, he developed a single-fiber ATPase assay, which he applies to screen new compounds for the pharmacological modulation of basal metabolism and to biopsies of patients to evaluate myosin energy consumption in hypermetabolic or hypometabolic conditions.

Dr. Léo BLERVAQUE serves as the scientific officer of the Metropole Savoie Hospital (Chambéry). His responsibilities encompass the development of clinical research within the institution, provision of methodological and scientific support to medical and paramedical staff, and management of the clinical research department. He contributed during his PhD in the PhyMedExp lab (INSERM-CNRS-Montpellier University) and his post-doc in the LIBM lab (Chambéry) to projects using muscle biopsies to assess changes in skeletal muscle capillarisation in chronic lung and sickle cell diseases, and their reversibility through exercise training. Additionally, he has collaborated with the French cycling and rowing federations on a project funded by the French National Agency for the Paris 2024 Olympic Games (THPCA2024) to elucidate the significance of muscle capillarisation for high performance. He is now scientifically engaged in several clinical studies, sponsored by the Métropole Savoie hospital, aimed at demonstrating the importance of addressing muscle deficiencies and systematizing exercise training in conditions like cancer or ICU stays.

Thomas Boudou is a CNRS researcher at the Laboratory for Interdisciplinary Physics in Grenoble. His research interests lie in understanding how cells interact with their environment, and how these interactions weigh on cellular processes. In particular, he is studying how the biochemical and mechanical properties of the microenvironment regulate cell adhesion, migration, differentiation and tissue formation. To this end, he is developing new approaches based on micro- and nanofabrication techniques to control and modulate the cell microenvironment. These engineered microsystems enable fundamental biological questions to be addressed (e.g. interactions extracellular matrix/growth factors, regulation of osteogenesis differentiation by material properties,...) as well as the development of new biomedical technologies (e.g. muscle on a chip, microcapsules for drug delivery,...). Recently, he has combined these microsystems with optogenetics to study the generation and propag ation of mechanical signals in tissue models.

Yan Burelle is University Research Chair in Integrative Mitochondrial Biology and Full Professor at the Faculty of Health Sciences and Medicine at the University of Ottawa in Canada (www.burellelab.org). He hold a PhD in Exercise Physiology from the Université de Montréal and completed his Post-Doctoral Training in Biochemistry at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver where he focused on understanding the mechanisms regulating energy production and shuttling in muscle cells. His lab integrates multiple facets of mitochondrial biology to gain a better understanding of their role in tissue plasticity and disease development. Beyond bioenergetics and metabolism, his lab investigates processes such as ROS metabolism and permeability transition pore opening, as well as mitochondrial quality control mechanisms. An important focus of his lab is to delineate the role of mitophagy in muscle stem cells, and test whether stimulation of this process can improve their regenerative capacity. Professor Burelle has received >12 M$ in total funding, published >80 research articles, and earned several research and career awards.

institution: Laboratoire de Biomécanique et Mécanique des Chocs

people.biosketch: Engineer in Mechanics and Ph.D. in Biomechanics, Laurence Chèze is Professor at University of Lyon 1 (France) where she is responsible of the Biomechanics specialty of the Master degree, and deputy-director of the laboratory LBMC. Her main fields of interest are multi-body modeling of the musculo-skeletal system, 3D motion experimental measurement and analysis. She has supervised 38 students in Ph.D., and published about 130 papers in peer-reviews journals and participated to more than 200 congresses (https://orcid.org/0000-0003-2265-9781).

Dr. Raphaël Dumas is Senior Researcher at Université Gustave Eiffel, working in the Laboratory of Biomechanics and Impact Mechanics (LBMC UMR_T9406), a joint research unit funded by Université Gustave Eiffel and Université Lyon 1. He is currently member of the board of the technical group 3-D Analysis of Human Movement of the International Society of Biomechanics. His area of expertise is multibody modelling of the musculoskeletal system, estimation of musculo-tendon, articular contact, and ligament forces from motion capture with validation against measurements obtained in vivo by instrumented implants. For example, he has developed subject-specific lower limb models based on medical images to predict articular contact forces in patients with osteoarthritis and patients with total hip or knee arthroplasty.

Thomas Christen is an INSERM researcher working at the Grenoble Institute of Neurosciences (Grenoble, France). His research focuses on the development of new Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) techniques to better understand the human brain functions and diagnose diseases. This includes better acquisition schemes (sequences, hardware) and post-processing algorithms. In particular, he works on new ways to accelerate MRI protocols using the "MR fingerprinting" method combined with Artificial Intelligence codes (ANR MRFUSE). In parallel, he develops new tools to probe tissue microstructures by combining multi-dimensional MRI acquisitions with deep learning and advanced numerical simulations.

Prof. Glenda Comai is a CNRS permanent researcher at the Stem Cells and Development Unit of Institute Pasteur in Paris. Her current research bridges the developmental biology and stem cells fields with focus on craniofacial muscles. Using 3D-imaging, mouse genetics and single cell/single nuclear omics she seeks to understand how heterogeneity at the level of stem cells and myofibres is established, and how this impacts on muscular genetic disorders. She has a long-term interest in the mechanisms underlying tissue patterning during development.

Prof. Katrien de Bock is a full professor and deputy head of the Department of Health Sciences and Technology at ETH Zürich. The De Bock laboratory focuses its research on investigating how endothelial cells rewire their metabolism during angiogenesis and how endothelial cells metabolically communicate with other cell types in the muscle microenvironment to maintain or establish muscle homeostasis. Specific interest goes to deciphering mechanisms of blood vessel growth and endothelial metabolic crosstalk in the muscle following exercise and/or muscle injury.

Dr Esteves De Lima is an academic researcher at INSERM. She works on skeletal muscle development and epigenetic regulation in the laboratory of Prof Relaix in Mondor Institut for Biomedical Research. She performed her doctoral training with Dr Delphine Duprez (IBPS, Paris) and Prof Carmen Birchmeier (MDC, Berlin). Throughout the years her research focus was on fundamental research with the use of skeletal muscle tissue and the myogenic program as a model to study diverse biological questions in a variety of animal models. She addressed questions that contributed to the understanding of how signaling pathway networks, mechano-transduction signals and chromatin architecture regulate muscle stem cell maintenance in development and adult systems. She now combines her expertise in epigenetic regulation, cell differentiation and mouse molecular tools to focus on how alterations in the chromatin architecture are implicated in cell identity, both in development and adult muscle regeneration contexts.

institution: Centre de Recherche en Cancérologie de Lyon

people.biosketch: Dr Céline Delloye-Bourgeois is a researcher at the CNRS and leader of the KidsCaN team at the Cancer Research Center of Lyon (CRCL). Her research is focused on functional interactions between fundamental embryogenic processes and the tumoral and metastatic properties of pediatric cancers, particularly those affecting the nervous system. Specifically, the team develops analytical pipelines combining micro-manipulations in the avian embryo, multi-scale imaging approaches and high depth single-cell and spatial omics data. Céline co-founded the startup Oncofactory, which has now become an ERBC company, that exploits the process of cancer cell micro-implantation in avian embryos to propose preclinical evaluation of anticancer therapies and in-depth characterization of therapy mechanisms of action for biomarker discovery and applications in personalized medicine.

Sylvain Dorel is Professor at the Nantes University (France), and a member of the Laboratory “Movement, Interactions, Performance” (MIP). He has a background in Human Movement Sciences and worked as researcher at the French National Institute for Sports (INSEP, France) from 2005 to 2010. His research focuses on muscle biomechanics, neuromuscular function in human and sport performance. The main field of his investigations is to better understand the motor function and its plasticity using a neuromechanical approach coupling the study of mechanical output, the muscle properties (e,g, the muscle-tendon interactions) and the muscle coordination (e,g, level and timing of activation). Several projects over the last 15 years concerned the Neuromechanics of multi-joint tasks (pedaling, running, and squat) with specific interest into the optimization of the maximal power and the top-level performance in cycling. In this context, he led different research projects funded by the French Ministry of Sport, and works in close collaboration with French Cycling Federation (FFC) and professional cycling team (Total Energie) from several years. He has been a Scientific Advisor for national track cycling team for the last three Olympic Games (2012-2021) and currently coordinates a work package in a French national agency grant project for the Paris 2024 Olympics (THPCA2024).

institution: Institut de Génomique Fonctionnelle de Lyon

people.biosketch: Prof. Jonathan Enriquez is group leader at Institute of Functional Genomics of Lyon (IGFL) at the Ecole Normal Supérieure of Lyon (ENSL), France. From 2010 to 2015 Dr Enriquez was postdoctoral Research Scientist at Columbia University, New York. In 2016, he obtained a permanent position at CNRS in France and started his own group in 2017 at IGFL. He uses Drosophila melanogaster to discover new biological concepts and mechanisms of development. His research combines genetics, molecular biology, imaging, post-imaging processing, computational biology, and behavioral approaches.

Karine Gauthier is a CNRS CRCN. She works at the IGFL in Lyon in the group “Functional genomics of thyroid hormone signaling”. She supervises projects aiming to understand how endogenous T3 signaling, in brain and peripheral metabolic tissues, is involved in regulating energy expenditure, using both tissue selective inhibition and activation of TR in mice. Her most recent works used a combination of mouse genetics, genomics and classical physiology, to determine how thyroid hormone signaling respectively in neurons and brown adipocytes impacts the thermogenic responses to cold exposure and western diet feeding. She is involved in many collaborations to study how TR regulate different aspects of metabolism in other tissues including skeletal muscle. In parallel she also serves as the “equality referent” of IGFL for the CNRS. In this context she has been trained on gender issues related to science.

Dr. Yad Ghavi-Helm is group leader at the Institute of Functional Genomics of Lyon (IGFL) at the Ecole Normale Supérieure of Lyon (ENSL), France. She performed her postdoctoral research at the European Molecular Biology Laboratory (EMBL) in Heidelberg (Germany) before obtaining a permanent position at the CNRS in 2017. She then established her team at the IGFL with the support from various starting grants including an ERC Starting Grant. Her team studies transcription regulation by developmental enhancers using Drosophila embryogenesis as a model system by combining genetics, genomics, imaging, and computational approaches.

Dr. Sabine Richard works at the Institut de Génomique Fonctionnelle de Lyon (ENS de Lyon) as an INRAE researcher. She is exploring various aspects of behavioral neuroscience, with a focus on mammals and birds. Dr. Richard thinks that understanding how animals perceive and emotionally deal with their environment is critical not only to improve human consideration of animals, but also to improve the conditions under which humans interact with and utilize animals in diverse contexts. Besides her research, after investigating farm animals' emotional repertoires, Dr. Richard actively participates in the ethical evaluation of projects involving live animals. She enjoys sharing her knowledge and engaging in meaningful discussions with students, colleagues, and the general public to raise awareness and understanding of animal behavior and welfare and more generally to make science accessible to as many people as possible.

Dr Ruggiero is Director of Research at the CNRS. She is a group leader at the Institute of Functional Genomics of Lyon (IGFL), a research department of the Ecole Normale Supérieure de Lyon, France. Her team combines functional genomics, biochemistry, microscopies and developmental biology to decode the functional specificity and the dynamics of extracellular matrices in development, regeneration and disease, specifically in the neuromuscular system and skin. She has authored over a hundred publications in the matrix biology field and was honored to serve as Chair (2017) for the Collagen Gordon Research Conference. Research funding of the team comes from a variety of sources, including academia, charities and industry. She was member of the executive team of the SFR Biosciences (2006-2011) and served as director of the IGFL (2016-2020). She is a past councilor of the International Society for Matrix Biology (ISMB) and the current president of the French Society for Matrix Biology (SFBMec).

Dr Marie Fabre is currently a post-doc at LIBM in Université Jean Monnet de Saint-Etienne under the supervision of Dr. Thomas Lapole. Her research activities focus on the study of sensorimotor mechanisms at the cortical and peripheral levels during movement. She is particularly interested in these mechanisms in postural control during balance maintenance and locomotion.  She is investigating the improvement of postural control by stimulating the proprioceptive system (with postural exercises and localized vibrations and/or electrical sensory stimulation) in elderly people and children with cerebral palsy. This last project is part of a European project funded by the ANR-Neuron with the Université Libre de Bruxelles and the University of Thessaloniki.

Prof. Damien Freyssenet is an exercise physiologist and biochemist, Professor at Jean Monnet University in Saint-Etienne. He is currently head of the Deconditioning Reconditioning of skeletal Muscle - Systemic Environment research team at the Laboratoire Interuniversitaire de Biologie de la Motricité. Damien Freyssenet's research activity focuses on the mechanisms of skeletal muscle deconditioning under physiological (dry immersion) and pathological (cancer, myopathies, sepsis) conditions, as well as on the development of strategies to limit/prevent this deconditioning. Damien Freyssenet has published 61 papers (citations > 6,000, H index 28). Damien Freyssenet is financially supported by the Association Française contre les Myopathies, the Fondation ARC pour la Recherche sur le Cancer, the Ligue contre le Cancer, or the Centre National des Études Spatiales.

Bénédicte Guégan is a PhD student working in the DEREM-SE team (Deconditionning Reconditionning of Muscle and Systemic Environment), under the supervision of Pr Damien Freyssenet at the LIBM (Laboratoire interuniversitaire de Biologie de la Motricité). During her master degree she worked in UMR-1124, on citrulline supplementation in obese older adults, under the supervision of Pr Philippe Noirez and in collaboration with the UQAM (Université du Québec à Montreal). She is currently on her second year of PhD leading her research on central inflammation in the physiopathological context of cancer cachexia in APC Min/+ mice. She is also an active member of animal welfare structure attached to the animal facility she is working with.

Pr Lafage-Proust was trained at University of Bordeaux , France & at Merck Research Lab USA. She is currently full professor at the University Jean Monnet (UJM), Saint-Etienne, where she teaches cell biology at the Medical School. She is physician at the Rheumatology Department of the University Hospital in St-Etienne. She takes care of patients with metabolic bone disorders, with a particular interest for patients with chronic kidney disease. She is also researcher at the INSERM 1059 unit SAINBIOSE, team "Biology of bone and joint tissues”. She is expert in the role of microvascularisation in bone remodelling and in response to osteo-anabolic stimuli such as parathormone as well as in the role of bone proteins of the SIBLING family and in particular of the bone sialoprotein (under the direction of L Malaval). She has 226 publications referenced in Clarivate Web of Science®. She is in charge of scientific integrity at the UJM since 2020. She was vice chancellor of the administrative council of UJM.

After obtaining his PhD in 2009 (University of Amiens), Thomas Lapole got a position of assistant professor at the University of Saint-Etienne in 2012. He was Dean of the Sport Science department (educational) (2016-2018) and was named Vice-Dean of the Inter-university Laboratory of Human Movement Biology in 2020. Dr Lapole mainly conducts research programs on the plasticity of neuromuscular function in response to local vibration. He also extended his thematic areas to the study of neuromuscular fatigue as well as neuromuscular electrical stimulation. He also developed works related to the evaluation of muscle mechanical properties. All these research activities have been well funded (over 1 000 000€ up to September 2021). In September 2021, Dr Lapole had published 57 journal articles and signed more than 70% of these publications in a significant rank of the authorship (1st, 2nd or last rank).

Dr Angèle Merlet is a university hospital assistant at Myology Unit in University Hospital of Saint-Etienne and at the Inter-university Laboratory of Human Movement Biology (LIBM) in Jean Monnet University of Saint Etienne. After a PhD in Biology and Exercise Physiology at the Jean Monnet University in 2018 on the benefits of endurance exercise training on skeletal muscle characteristics in sickle cell disease patients, she worked on medullar neurophysiology and locomotor control at Sherbrooke University (Québec, Canada). Her current work is based on the benefits of tailored physical activity (multiple sclerosis, neuromuscular diseases) and on the exploration of muscle tissue (in pathological conditions or for high-level performance).

Prof. Millet was named at the ‘Institut Universitaire de France’ as a Senior member in 2019. His general research area investigates the physiological, neurophysiological and biomechanical factors associated with fatigue, both during extreme exercise and in patients (neuromuscular diseases, cancer, ICU). His research is focusing on understanding fatigue in order to create tailored rehabilitation programs for clinical populations and enhance patients’ quality of life. In December 2021, he had published 5 books and 260 journal articles (cited > 11,300 times), his H index was 58. He has supervised 40 postdoctoral fellows and PhD students coming from 13 different countries and he served as an external reviewer for over 60 PhD candidates. Guillaume has been an invited speaker 135 times in 17 different countries.

Jean-Benoit Morin is Full Professor at the University of Saint-Etienne (France), and a member of the Interuniversity Laboratory of Human Movement Biology (LIBM). He is also associate researcher with the Sports Research Institute New-Zealand at Auckland University of Technology, and visiting Professor in Locomotion Biomechanics at Loughborough University. He obtained a Track & Field Coach National Diploma in 1998 and a Ph.D. in Human Locomotion and Performance in 2004. His field of research is mainly human locomotion and performance, with specific interest in running biomechanics and maximal power movements (sprint, jumps). He has edited a textbook (Biomechanics of Training and Testing, Springer, 2018) and published over 150 peer-reviewed scientific papers. He is also a consultant for professional sports groups (soccer, rugby, sprint…).

Dr Vianney Rozand, PhD, is an assistant professor at Jean Monnet University in Saint Etienne and a member of the ActiFS (Physical Activity, Fatigue, Health) academic chair led by Pr Guillaume Millet. After a PhD in Exercise Physiology from the University of Burgundy in 2015, he specialized in neuromuscular fatigue with aging during his post-doc at Marquette University (Milwaukee, USA) with Pr Sandra Hunter. His current work at the Inter-university Laboratory of Human Movement Biology (LIBM) is on the evolution of neuromuscular function and fatigability in old and very old adults (> 80 yrs), and the influence of physical activity on the maintenance of these capacities. He is also director of the Master degree of Evaluation and Engineering of Sport Performance.

Prof. Laurence VICO is a physiologist, Research Director at INSERM, working at Jean Monnet University in Saint-Etienne. She leads the SAINBIOSE Unit (INSERM U1059) which includes two teams, one working on cardiovascular diseases, the other on osteoarticular diseases. Her research themes on the skeletal system encompasses the understanding of the mechanical and metabolic deconditioning occurring in extreme (spaceflight and analogs) or disuse (osteoporosis, inactivity, nutrition disorders) conditions. Such (dys)adaptations encompass intertwined loops leading to bone loss, vascular changes, muscle shift and metabolic alterations. Another target is the effects of pharmaceutical or physical training strategies and their safe and efficient application to frail subjects. Laurence Vico has published more than 300 papers (citations > 8,000, H index 53) and is financially supported by the ANR, the European Agency or the Centre National des Études Spatiales.

Dr Jerome N. Feige is the head of the Physical Health department and vice-director of the Nestlé Institute of Health Sciences in Lausanne, Switzerland, and a recognized expert in muscle and aging biology. He holds a degree in Bioengineering and a PhD in Biology from the University of Lausanne. Dr Feige performed post-doctoral research at the Institute of Genetics, and Molecular and Cellular Biology in Strasbourg, France on the molecular regulation of energy metabolism. He subsequently worked as laboratory head at the Novartis Institute of Biomedical Research in Basel, Switzerland, where he performed drug discovery for muscle diseases and contributed to the development of new therapies. Since 2012, Dr Feige has held increasing responsibilities in the Nestlé Institute of Health Sciences where he established a research program studying muscle biology and a translational department developing nutritional therapies to support the Musculo-Skeletal system. His research programs have led to the commercialization of several products for infant and medical nutrition, and to the creation of 2 start-ups. Dr Feige is also an adjunct lecturer at the Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) where he teaches nutrition and entrepreneurship, and trains PhD students in biomedical science.

Pr Béatrice Fervers (MD, PhD, Associate Professor in Oncology), heads the Prevention Cancer Environment Department at the Léon Bérard Cancer Centre, Lyon, and is deputy Director of the INSERM Unit 1296 'Radiations: Defense, Health, Environment'. Pr. Beatrice Fervers directs since 2010 a physical activity program for cancer patients with a dedicated space of 300m² and a team of physicians, adapted physical activity trainers, dieticians, PhD students and post-doctoral researchers, managing since 2018 over 1000 patients per year. Pr Fervers has extensive expertise in coordinating interdisciplinary research in cancer primary and tertiary prevention, in particular interventional research in exercise oncology. About 500 cancer patients have been included in exercise trials in the past three years and four trials are currently open for inclusion .

Manon Gouez is a PhD student in exercise physiology and oncology in Cancer Prevention and Environment, Léon Bérard Cancer Center (Lyon) and in Inter-University Laboratory of Human Movement Biology (Team « Atherosclerosis, Thrombose et Physical Activity »). Her primary interest is the interaction between acute physical exercise and imuno-chemotherapy in metastatic lung cancer patients (ERICA clinical study NCT04676009). She also investigates the effect of treadmill running on the tumor growth and the potential underlying anticancer mechanisms (intratumoral immune cells infiltration and hypoxia) in a mouse model.

institution: Institut NeuroMyoGène - Appui à la recherche

people.biosketch: Dr. Gache is a CRCN INSERM researcher and lead the “Muscle Nuclear & Cytoskeleton Architecture Team” at the NeuroMyoGene Institute (INMG) in Lyon. Dr Gache is a member of the Scientific Society board of the French Society of Myology (SFM), was the recipient of the competitive ATIP-Avenir program (2014) and has a recognized expertise on cytoarchitecture, gene expression and muscle cell homeostasis. He has developed a long partnership with the “Association Française contre les myopathies” (AFM) and is financially supported by various organisms (MyoNeurAlp-AFM, Phenomin, ANR, INMG-CNMD, Maladies rare, RHU) to developed his science. MNCA team is highly focused on understanding mechanisms controlling cytoskeleton rearrangements, myonuclear domain establishment & maintenance during muscle differentiation and their implication in pathological contexts such as genetic disorders (Centronuclear myopathies, cardiomyopathies) or physiological aging (Sarcopenia).

Julien Gondin (PhD) is a CNRS researcher at Institut NeuroMyoGène (Lyon) where he leads the research group “electrostimulation and cachexia” in the Chazaud Team (www.musclestem.com). He has a recognized experience in the evaluation of skeletal muscle function in both human and animals. Over the last 15 years, his research interests focused on the acute and chronic effects of neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) thanks to multidisciplinary methodologies (force measurements, proteomics, MRI...). His research group now focuses on the effectiveness of carefully-controlled NMES training protocols for minimizing muscle dysfunctions in two pathologies (i.e., cancer and critical illness myopathy). Dr Gondin has published 65 papers (H-index: 20). Dr Gondin is financially supported by the European program on rare diseases, Association Française contre les Myopathies, the Fondation ARC pour la Recherche sur le Cancer, the Ligue contre le Cancer and the Canceropôle CLARA

Dr Jacquemond has a long-standing research experience and expertise in the field of Ca2+ signaling and excitation-contraction coupling in muscle, with a dedicated focus on the use of single muscle cell physiology and biophysics techniques to investigate the live function of the mechanisms that regulate these processes. He developed a most efficient combination of voltage-clamp and fluorescent imaging on native differentiated muscle fibers, allowing control and quantitative assessment of the function of these processes at the cellular and subcellular level. His contributions to the field cover a wide range of interests including – the physiological properties of ryanodine receptors activity in normal conditions and under various conditions of stress, – the mechanisms in process during muscle diseases such as Duchenne dystrophy, centronuclear myopathies, ryanodinopathies, – signaling within sub-cellular compartments of the muscle cells using targeted, genetically-encoded biosensing fluorescent probes.

Dr Arnaud Jacquier is a hospital and university assistant in the team “nerve–muscle interaction” of Pr Laurent Schaeffer at the NeuroMyoGene institute. He is the head of the iPS core facility of the institute. His area of expertise is neuromuscular disorders, especially affecting the motoneuron or the neuromuscular junction. His research focuses on the development and characterization of in vitro models to prove the pathogenicity of genetic variants of unknown significance. He recently identified for the first time a mutation in COQ7 gene associated with distal hereditary motor neuropathy that is potentially treatable, paving the way for innovative therapeutics in the field.

Charline Jomard started her scientific career with a technical diploma at the University of Avignon and then graduated from the engineering school Polytech Marseille in Biological Engineering. After one year as a Project Engineer, she decided to go back to science to complete a PhD. She is currently in her third year of PhD in the team of Bénédicte Chazaud at the Institut NeuroMyoGene in Lyon (INMG PNMG CNRS 5261 - INSERM U1315 - UCBL1), working under the supervision of Julien Gondin on the impact of sex and estrogens on the mechanistic of skeletal muscle regeneration at the functional and cellular levels. Her work was awarded on two international congresses.

Dr Anita Kneppers is a postdoctoral researcher working in the team of Rémi Mounier at Institute NeuroMyoGène. She studies the metabolic regulation of skeletal muscle stem cell fate, and particularly their contribution to myonuclear accretion. This research interest logically follows her initial training as a clinical nutritionist, and her contribution to research as part of the ‘Human and Animal Physiology’ and the ‘Nutrition, Metabolism and Genomics’ groups in the Wageningen, The Netherlands. Subsequently, she performed her PhD studies addressing the regulation of skeletal muscle recovery in patients with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) at Maastricht University in The Netherlands. In 2019, she joined the team of Rémi Mounier in Lyon as a postdoc, to study the role of the metabolic checkpoint AMPKα2 in cell-cell communication leading to cell fusion.

Rémi Mounier is currently head of the Team "Metabolic regulations of adult muscle stem cells" in Institut Neuromyogène. His research highlighted intracellular crosstalk between metabolism and inflammation during muscle regeneration. In this context, they decipher the role of metabolism on muscle stem cells by investigating metabolic regulations of their fate, particularly the role of AMPK and the metabolic characteristics of muscle stem cells. The goal of his program is to determine the dynamic interactions between metabolism and muscle stem cell fate during muscle plasticity and return to homeostasis. Rémi Mounier has published 73 papers (citations > 4500, H-index = 36). His team has been supported by the Association Française contre les Myopathies, the Ligue contre le Cancer, the Fondation pour la Recherche Médicale and the European Union.

Dr. Hélène Puccio is a Inserm Research Director and heads a research laboratory focusing on recessive ataxia, a group of heterogeneous movement disorders. Since 1998, her laboratory was located at the IGBMC, Strasbourg (France), and she has recently moved her laboratory to the Institut NeuroMyoGène (INMG), Lyon (France) (https://www.inmg.fr/puccio/?lang=en). Her research interest focuses on understanding the pathophysiological mechanisms implicated in recessive ataxias linked to mitochondrial dysfunction, discovering disease biomarkers and developing therapeutic approaches. Her team has made significant contributions advancing fundamental knowledge on Fe-S cluster and CoQ10 biosynthesis, pathophysiological pathways involved in Friedreich ataxia and COQ8A-ataxia, and developing novel therapeutic approaches, including gene therapy approaches.

Dr. Lorenzo Giordani is a researcher at Sorbonne University specialized in muscle biology and bioinformatics. His expertise is particularly focused on spatial biology and single-cell modeling. After earning his Master’s degree from the University of Rome Tor Vergata, he moved to California to pursue a PhD under the supervision of Dr. Puri at the Sanford Burnham Institute. Upon completing his PhD, he returned to Europe, where he continued his research as a postdoctoral fellow, first at the Cochin Institute and then at the Centre de Recherche en Myologie. In 2020, Dr. Giordani was awarded an ANR JCJC grant, enabling him to establish his own lab. His research group currently investigates the cellular heterogeneity of muscle tissue and seeks to uncover the molecular mechanisms underpinning muscle function and pathology. With a focus on Duchenne and Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophies, Dr. Giordani’s team integrates bioinformatics and cellular biology to deepen understanding of these conditions and explore potential therapeutic pathways.

Prof. Eglantine Heude is a permanent CNRS researcher expert in Developmental and Evolutionary Biology. She has just created her team at the “Institut de Génomique Fonctionnelle de Lyon” (ENS de Lyon, September 2024) to develop her own research thematic investigating the developmental and evolutionary origins of tetrapods. Since her PhD, she has focused on the cellular and molecular mechanisms at the origin of a functional and integrated musculoskeletal system in vertebrates. The current research axes combine functional genomics, transcriptomics, comparative embryology and comparative anatomy approaches by studying different conventional and unconventional vertebrate models. Her team seeks to elucidate the morphogenetic bases of morphological innovations and musculoskeletal adaptions to new environments. Eglantine Heude has published 22 papers (citations > 800, H index 17). She is financially supported by the French National Research Agency for young researchers (ANR JCJC).

Dr Cameron Hill is a postdoctoral research associate at King’s College London, UK, within the Randall Centre for Cell and Molecular Biophysics. Prior to this role, he worked as a research technician in the Structure and Motion Laboratory at the Royal Veterinary College, UK, (2017–2019), where he employed kinematic video analysis, X-ray Reconstruction of Moving Morphology (XROMM), and musculoskeletal robotics to investigate anuran locomotion. Cameron holds a BSc in Sport and Exercise Science from Coventry University, UK, (2011–2014) and completed his PhD at the same institution (2014–2018), examining the effects of ageing and obesity on isometric force, work loop power output, and fatigue resistance of isolated locomotor and respiratory skeletal muscle. His current research uses synchrotron-based, time-resolved small-angle X-ray diffraction to probe the regulatory states of myosin-containing thick filaments and actin-containing thin filaments in skeletal muscle during contraction. This work focuses on phenotypic differences between fast- and slow-twitch muscle across a range of contractile paradigms, including twitch and tetanic contraction, unloaded shortening, active stretch, length-step perturbations, and force–velocity profiling. He is also interested in how disease models, including ageing and obesity, impair contractile function at the cellular level, and in developing strategies to restore muscle performance.

Dr. Gabrielle Kardon is a professor at the University of Utah whose lab studies skeletal muscle development, regeneration, response to viral infection, and evolution. Always interested in evolution, she initially studied geology and paleontology at Yale University and then at the University of Michigan. After learning about the important role of Hox genes in regulating development and evolution, she switched her research focus to developmental biology. At Duke University, with mentorship from David McClay and Stephen Wainwright, she completed her PhD on the development of limb muscle and tendons, using the chick as a model system. She did postdoctoral training with Cliff Tabin at Harvard Medical School, where she began investigating the role of interactions between muscle and muscle connective tissue fibroblasts in the development of limb muscle. Since 2004, she has had an independent lab at the University of Utah. The lab studies the development of the essential mammalian muscle, the diaphragm, and the genetic and cellular causes of the common birth defect, Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernias. The lab also investigates the cellular and molecular processes regulating adult muscle regeneration after acute, sterile injury. Finally, we have also expanded our research into discovering how infection by mosquito-borne alphaviruses – a major and growing health concern – causes acute and chronic muscle weakness.

institution: Institut de Biologie de l'École Normale Supérieure

people.biosketch: Dr Alice Meunier is CNRS Director of Research at the Institut de Biologie de l’ENS. With insightful students and colleagues, she combined cell biology, different kind of microscopies and developmental biology to understand how multiciliated cells escape the centriole number control program to massively amplify these organelles during their differentiation, and form the ciliary tuft required to propel physiological fluids. They showed that instead of implementing a specific developmental program, they reuse the actors of centriole duplication and cell division to carry out their differentiation. They are now seeking to characterize the actors of this cell cycle diversion. Alice Meunier was also formally associated professor at Ecole Polytechnique in charge of teaching biotechnologies. She resigned after realizing that the knowledge produced by fundamental research in biology could be used for the better, but also for the worst, and that the acceleration we are observing in our everyday life, was also touching the research community. She therefore decided to dedicate part of her time to explore how to make a research respecting the equilibrium of ecosystems, and compatible with a convivial human society. To educate herself in this direction, she got involved in different research communities (mouvement pour les savoirs engagés et reliés, écopolien, scientifiques en rébellion, labo1p5).

Dr Baptiste Morel is Associate Professor at University Savoie Mont-Blanc (Chambéry), working in the Inter-University Laboratory of Human Movement Biology (LIBM). His research investigates fatigue phenomenon at the interface of muscle physiology and biomechanics with applications in the domains of health, sports performance, and ecology. In particular, he develops a conceptual framework and a mathematical model of the force-velocity-endurance relationship. In this context, he is Principal Investigator of the interdisciplinary projects BIOCARE FActory (building a biopsychosocial model of cancer related fatigue) and FOVEAL (ANR - Force-velocity-endurance in animal locomotion). He also collaborates with several professional sports structures (LOU Rugby, AG2R La Mondiale) and the french cycling and rowing federations within a French national agency grant project for the Paris 2024 Olympics (THPCA2024).

institution: Institut des Maladies Métaboliques et Cardiovasculaires

people.biosketch: Dr Cedric Moro is currently Research Director at Inserm, and head of the Team MetaDiab “Pathophysiology of Metabolic Disorders and Diabesity” at the Institute of Metabolic and Cardiovascular Diseases in Toulouse. He holds a PhD and habilitation (HDR) in pathophysiology. Cedric Moro’s research uses a highly translational medicine approach to study the determinants and molecular mechanisms of adipose tissue and skeletal muscle health, metabolic dysfunction and insulin resistance in various pathological contexts (Sedentarity, Aging, Obesity and Type 2 diabetes). He has published 117 original articles and 18 review articles in the field of metabolism, exercise, skeletal muscle and adipose tissue biology (citations>7000, h-index 45). His research is currently supported by Inserm, Fondation pour la Recherche Médicale, Agence Nationale de la Recherche, Société Francophone du Diabète, European Federation for the Study of Diabetes, Joint Programme Initiative Healthy Diet for a Healthy Lifestyle, Région Occitanie, and IHU HealthAge.

institution: Foundation for People with Rare Diseases

people.biosketch: Dr Pauline Nauroy is head of the scientific policy at the Foundation For Rare Diseases, Paris, France. She did a PhD at the Institut de Génomique Fonctionnelle de Lyon in Lyon, France, and then pursues her academic career by doing a post-doctorate at the University of Freiburg, Germany, both on extracellular matrix, skin biology and pathologies. In her current position, Pauline Nauroy is leading the scientific strategy of the Foundation For Rare Diseases through interaction with French and European rare diseases ecosystem. She implements and manages call for proposals, follows research projects financed by the Foundation and detects and supports therapeutical proof of concepts in order to promote the research on rare disease and help the development of new therapies for rare diseases.

Dr Blandine Poulet is a Senior Lecturer at the University of Liverpool, alongside her role as Deputy Head of Department and Education Lead. Her lab, currently composed of 2 post-docs and 2 masters students, uses preclinical murine models of disease to focus on determining mechanisms of joint degeneration during osteoarthritis. More specifically, her group is interested in how all tissues of the musculoskeletal system interact and promote OA development, and the role of specific extracellular matrix proteins in joint health and disease (such as Fibrillin-1). In parallel, Dr Poulet's research works to refine mouse models of OA to increase their translation to human disease; this includes the role of age, sex and menopause. Active funding includes major grants from the UK Medical Research Council (£1.1M as PI; £800k as co-PI). She has published so far 24 primary published papers, with H-index of 18 and 999 citations (Scopus).

Pavan Ramdya, Firmenich Next Generation Chair of Neuroengineering, is the Director of the Neuroengineering Laboratory at EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland. Dr. Ramdya received his PhD in Neurobiology from Harvard University and then performed postdoctoral work in Robotics and Neurogenetics at EPFL and UNIL, then Bioengineering at Caltech. His laboratory aims to draw inspiration from animals in order to design more intelligent and adaptive artificial systems. To accomplish this, they use computational, engineering, genetic, and microscopy approaches to investigate how neural population dynamics, biomechanics, and gene expression sculpt complex limb-dependent behaviors in Drosophila melanogaster. In recognition of his work, he has been awarded an HFSP Career Development Award, a Swiss National Science Foundation Eccellenza Grant, the UNIL Young Investigator Award in Basic Science, and is a member of the FENS-Kavli Network of Excellence.

Vanina Romanello is an assistant professor in general pathology at the University of Padova and a researcher at the Venetian Institute of Molecular Medicine in Padova. She has a long track record investigating the mechanisms that control muscle mass in health and disease. Over the last ten years, she has focused on studying mitochondria quality control pathways, establishing a causal link between muscle-specific mitochondrial network alterations, muscle loss, and Fgf21-dependent disruption of whole-body homeostasis. Moreover, she showed that Fgf21 is a novel player in mitophagy and muscle loss. Her team is currently focused on investigating novel metabolic players involved in maintaining muscle health, such as the role of the peroxisomal mitochondrial interaction in muscle function in health and disease.

institution: Laboratoire de recherche en cardiovasculaire, métabolisme, diabétologie et nutrition

people.biosketch: Sophie ROME is Director of Research at INRAe institute in the department of Human Nutrition. She is working in the laboratory of 'Cardiology, Metabolism, Nutrition & Diabetes' (CarMeN) in Lyon. She is interested in the molecular mechanisms that alter the skeletal muscle mass in the context of obesity and type 2 diabetes using omics technologies. She now focuses her work on the role of extracellular vesicles (EVs) released by skeletal muscle in the cross-talks between muscle and the other insulin-sensitive tissues, and on the impact of the diet on the composition and biological activity of muscle EVs. Her pioneering work in the field of metabolism has provided important data on the role of muscle EVs during muscle development, and on the alterations of muscle homeostasis in obesity and type 2 diabetes. She was president of the French Society for Extracellular vesicles (2017-2021) and 2 times co-chairs for the organization of the ISEV international meetings (2021-2022).

institution: Laboratoire d'Ecologie des Hydrosystèmes Naturels et Anthropisés

people.biosketch: Pr Damien Roussel is Professor at the university Claude Bernard in Lyon, working in the field of comparative physiology in the LEHNA laboratory. His research investigates how organisms (endotherms and ectotherms) adjust their mitochondrial activity and efficiency to overcame energy challenges imposed by nutritional (e.g. fasting), physiological (e.g. high locomotor activity, diving) and environmental constraints (e.g. cold, hypoxia). In particular, he is studying the skeletal muscle energetic adjustments of sea-acclimatized king penguin facing expansive energy consuming processes (endurance swimming, thermogenesis) with limited environmental resources (oxygen during active dives or nutriment while fasting several months during winter). In this context, he is Principal Investigator of the scientific program PHYSIONERGY of the French Polar institute (IPEV).

institution: Novo Nordisk Foundation Center for Basic Metabolic Research

people.biosketch: My research focuses on defining the molecular and physiological mechanisms by which diet, physical activity, and weight loss improve insulin sensitivity and protect against cardiometabolic diseases. Over the past two decades, I have established a strong research program centered on skeletal muscle biology, inter-organ communication, and the role of NAD⁺ metabolism in metabolic health. My group has pioneered work on NAD⁺ biosynthesis and consumption across multiple tissues, including muscle, liver, adipose tissue, and hypothalamus, revealing critical pathways that maintain tissue function and systemic energy homeostasis.
